references.text: The context of the ransom: an ox that gorges someone to death, and the owner knew it was dangerous
The prohibition against taking a ransom (כֹּפֶר) for a murderer's life shows the contrast to this law where ransom is permitted
Uses the term פִּדְיוֹן (ransom) for the soul, and discusses the price to redeem a life
Uses כֹּפֶר in connection with appeasing someone who has been wronged
A man's life can be redeemed with wealth, פִּדְיוֹן נַפְשׁוֹ
The wicked becomes a כֹּפֶר (ransom) for the righteous
God gives nations as a כֹּפֶר (ransom) for Israel
God finds a כֹּפֶר (ransom) to save humanity from the grave
Warning that a large ransom cannot save one from God's judgment
Jesus gave his life as a λύτρον (ransom) for many, fulfilling the principle of ransom
The Son of Man came to give his life as a λύτρον (ransom) for many
Christ gave himself as an ἀντίλυτρον (ransom) for all
Believers were redeemed (ἐλυτρώθητε) with Christ's precious blood, like a lamb without blemish
Typological connection: The legal possibility of paying ransom for life in the Mosaic Law is fulfilled theologically in Christ's sacrifice as a ransom price for all.
